A common myth! The idea that the Great Wall of China is visible from space has been debunked by astronauts and satellite images. While it's true that the wall is long and stretches across mountains and valleys, it's actually quite narrow and blends in with the surrounding terrain.

In reality, the Great Wall of China is only about 30 feet (10 meters) wide, and it's built on hills and mountains, which means it can't be seen from space. In fact, most of the wall is not even visible from low Earth orbit, where most satellites fly.

The myth that the Great Wall is visible from space likely originated from a 1938 book by a German writer named Willy Ley, who wrote that the wall was visible from the moon. This idea was later popularized in science fiction films and books, but it's been consistently contradicted by astronauts and satellite images.

In reality, many of the most notable structures in China are only visible from low Earth orbit or higher, such as the Three Gorges Dam or the city of Shanghai. The Great Wall of China is actually best seen on the ground, where its unique architecture and location make it a remarkable sight to behold.
